St. Alexis of Wilkes-Barre

Introduction

St. Alexis Toth is remembered as a priest and defender of Orthodoxy in North America. The published life describes his Eastern Catholic background, education, bereavement, and reception into the Orthodox Church, followed by ministry among immigrant communities. It recounts his work in several American cities and the later veneration of his relics at Saint Tikhon's Monastery.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

St. Alexis Toth came from a Carpatho-Russian Eastern Catholic family and was ordained a married priest. He lost both his wife and their child. His work before America included teaching church history and canon law, administration, and responsibility for an orphanage.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative, source anchor “Rosalie”

Life and notable events

Sent to Minneapolis in 1889, Alexis encountered rejection from the Latin-rite bishop John Ireland. He and his parish subsequently sought reception into Orthodoxy. Later he served at Wilkes-Barre and guided other immigrant parishes into the Orthodox Church.

[2] Ecclesiastical history or testimony · Hopko, The Spread of Orthodoxy in the Lower 48 States; St. Alexis Toth and his parishes

The OCA church-history account specifies that in 1891 Bishop Vladimir received Alexis and 361 parishioners into Orthodoxy. It then describes the Wilkes-Barre parish’s decision and his sixteen years of service there.

[2] Ecclesiastical history or testimony · Hopko, The Spread of Orthodoxy in the Lower 48 States; Conversion of the Uniates

Death and martyrdom

Illness worsened late in 1908. After seeking recuperation at the New Jersey shore, he returned to Wilkes-Barre and died on May 7, 1909. The life describes declining health.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative, source anchor “1908”

Writings and legacy

He is remembered as a defender and organizer of Orthodox life among Carpatho-Russian immigrants. His story includes both parish decisions and years of practical pastoral work.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative, source anchor “Carpatho-Russian”
